content.title: About
content.content: A chocolate cupcake without icing is a small, moist piece of cake infused with cocoa, without any additional topping. It delivers a rich chocolate flavor, a tender crumb, and a slightly wet texture, making it an ideal treat for pure chocolate lovers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cupcakes without icing are often served in cafés as a quick snack or coffee accompaniment.
Traditional chocolate cupcakes are made from flour, sugar, eggs, butter, and cocoa powder.
Skipping the icing reduces sugar and calorie content compared to frosted versions.
Cocoa used in the cupcake is rich in antioxidants that may support heart health.
In some regions these are called "plain" or "naked" chocolate cupcakes.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa contains flavonoids that help combat free radicals and support vascular function.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in cocoa contributes to muscle and nerve function and helps regulate blood sugar.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Chocolate cupcakes can aid in maintaining normal hemoglobin levels thanks to a modest iron content.

items.title: Provides some fiber
items.content: When whole‑grain flour is used, the cupcake adds dietary fiber beneficial for digestion.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates and a small amount of fat offers a quick and sustained source of energy.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Standard recipes use wheat flour, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Even without icing, sugar is still present; those monitoring blood glucose should watch portion size.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Cocoa contains small amounts of caffeine, which may affect sleep in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The cupcake remains calorie‑dense due to butter and sugar; moderation is key for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cupcake on its own, split it and top with fresh berries, ice cream, or yogurt. It also travels well in a lunchbox as a quick snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cupcake in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate (up to 1 week) or freeze (up to 2 months). Let it come to room temperature before serving.

chicken-drumstick-baked-broiled-or-roast.title: Chicken drumstick, baked, broiled, or roasted, skin eaten, from raw

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken drumsticks are the meat from the lower leg of a chicken, commonly prepared by baking, broiling, or grilling. The skin is edible and adds flavor and crispness. The meat is a rich source of high‑quality protein, B‑vitamins, and minerals such as iron and zinc.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Drumsticks are a staple in many world cuisines, from American BBQ to Asian curries.
The skin holds most of the fat, which becomes crispy and aromatic when cooked properly.
Roasting at 200 °C (400 °F) yields a golden crust in about 35‑45 minutes.
Drumsticks are usually cheaper than breast meat but are prized for their flavor and juiciness.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides roughly 20 g of complete protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Contains iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for immune health, bone strength, and enzymatic reactions.

items.title: Collagen source
items.content: The skin and connective tissue are good sources of collagen, which may benefit skin and joint health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Chicken drumsticks contain virtually no carbs, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Raw chicken can harbor Salmonella and Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F).

items.title: High skin fat content
items.content: The skin is high in saturated fat; people monitoring cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Histamine formation
items.content: Improper storage can lead to histamine buildup, causing food intolerance.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drumsticks can be baked, pan‑fried, grilled, or braised. Trim excess fat and pat the skin dry before cooking for extra crispness. Marinades of olive oil, lemon juice, garlic, and herbs enhance flavor. Serve with vegetables, potatoes, or whole‑grain sides.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw drumsticks refrigerated at +2‑4 °C for up to 2 days, or freeze at –18 °C for up to 9 months. Cooked drumsticks store in the fridge for 3‑4 days. Discard if they develop an off‑odor, slimy texture, or discoloration.

ham-or-pork-with-mushroom-sauce.title: Ham or Pork with Mushroom Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Ham or selected pork cuts simmered in a delicate mushroom sauce made from cream and aromatic button mushrooms. The dish offers a rich meaty flavor complemented by a creamy‑mushroom aroma, suitable as a hot main course with sides or as a standalone dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mushroom sauce is often prepared with cream, white wine, and fresh herbs, giving it a velvety texture.
Traditionally smoked ham is used, but fresh pork can be substituted after searing.
Button mushrooms used in the sauce are rich in B‑vitamins and minerals such as selenium and potassium.
The dish is popular in European cuisine, especially in Scandinavian and Central European countries.
It is commonly garnished with fresh parsley or dill before serving.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Ham and pork provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms and meat supply B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Pork and ham are good sources of heme iron, important for normal blood formation.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: Selenium present in mushrooms contributes to immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: The creamy sauce adds calcium and phosphorus, vital for bone and tooth health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham is often salty; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Pork and cream can be high in saturated fats, which may be unsuitable for cardiovascular conditions.

items.title: Mushroom allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms.

items.title: Requires proper cooking
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor pathogens, so ensure the meat is fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, paired with mashed potatoes, rice, pasta, or vegetable sides. A sprinkle of fresh herbs or a splash of lemon juice can brighten the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C. It can be frozen for up to 2 months, preferably portioned beforehand.

content.title: About
content.content: Pepperoni pizza is a popular fast‑food option made with a thin, crispy crust, tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, and slices of spicy pepperoni sausage. The pepperoni adds a distinctive aroma and mild heat, while the thin crust keeps the dish light and crunchy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “pepperoni” is Italian for “peppers,” but in the U.S. it refers to a spicy pork or beef sausage.
Thin‑crust pizza originated in Naples in the 19th century and became a staple of New York‑style pizzerias.
The combination of tomato sauce and mozzarella provides a good source of lycopene and calcium.
Pepperoni pizza is often considered a comfort food and is a common late‑night order.
In the United States, over 30 % of all pizza sales include pepperoni.

items.title: High in Protein
items.content: Pepperoni and cheese supply high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium Source
items.content: Mozzarella cheese contains calcium that supports bone and dental health.

items.title: Lycopene in Tomato Sauce
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that may reduce the risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The sausage and dough provide B1, B2, and B6 vitamins important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Quick Energy
items.content: The thin crust and moderate fat content make this pizza a fast source of calories.

items.title: High Sodium Content
items.content: Pepperoni and sauce often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated Fats
items.content: Cheese and sausage add saturated fats, which should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Dairy Allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy should choose a dairy‑free cheese alternative.

items.title: Spicy Food Sensitivity
items.content: Pepperoni may irritate the stomach of individuals with gastritis or ulcer disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pepperoni pizza is typically enjoyed hot, cut into slices. You can add fresh vegetables, basil, or a drizzle of olive oil for extra flavor. Some like to serve it with ranch or garlic dip.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore the crisp crust. It can be frozen for up to 2 months if wrapped tightly in plastic.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef pot pie is a baked dish featuring tender chunks of stewed beef, vegetables, and a savory broth encased in a flaky crust. It is traditionally cooked in a ceramic or metal dish, resulting in a golden, crisp topping.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meat pies became popular in the United States in the early 19th century as a convenient way to use leftover stew.
The classic crust is made from flour, butter, water, and sometimes eggs, giving it a layered texture.
Typical fillings include carrots, peas, and potatoes alongside the beef.
Individual ceramic ramekins are often used to serve pot pies, keeping them warm and aromatic.
In some regions the dish is nicknamed “black pie” because of the dark‑browned crust.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: The heme iron in beef is readily absorbed and helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef pot pie supplies B12, B6, and niacin, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Vegetable‑derived fiber
items.content: Carrots, peas, and potatoes add dietary fiber that promotes regular digestion.

items.title: Balanced energy
items.content: The combination of protein, fat, and carbohydrates provides sustained satiety.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Traditional recipes use butter and fatty beef, which can raise cholesterol if consumed frequently.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Salt is added for flavor; individuals with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The crust is usually made from wheat flour, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Proper heating
items.content: Undercooked pie may harbor bacteria; ensure the interior reaches at least 74 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the beef pot pie hot, cutting it into individual portions. It pairs well with a simple green salad, a dollop of sour cream, or plain yogurt. Leftovers should be refrigerated and reheated in the oven to retain a crisp crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the pie to room temperature, then place it in an airtight container and store in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags for up to 2 months. Reheat at 180 °C until the crust is golden before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato is a tuber harvested from the plant Solanum tuberosum. A hash brown is a dish made from grated or shredded potato that is fried until golden and crisp. Product NFS (4237) is a ready‑to‑eat hash brown packaged in individual portions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes were introduced to Europe from South America in the 16th century.
The hash brown originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a popular breakfast item.
Frying creates a crunchy exterior while keeping the interior tender.
NFS (4237) is produced using flash‑freezing technology to preserve flavor and nutrients.
More than 300 million tonnes of potatoes are consumed worldwide each year.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes provide complex carbs that supply sustained energy and promote satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain vitamin B6 and B3, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are a good source of potassium, helping maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Shredded potato in hash browns retains some fiber, aiding digestive health.

items.title: Low fat when prepared properly
items.content: When fried with a modest amount of oil, hash browns remain relatively low‑calorie.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to potatoes.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared hash browns often contain added salt; low‑sodium options are recommended for those with hypertension.

items.title: Oil degradation during frying
items.content: Reusing frying oil can produce harmful compounds; it is best to use fresh oil for each batch.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the hash brown in a skillet, oven, or microwave. Serve as a side dish with meat, as a breakfast with eggs, or incorporate into salads and sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the packaged hash brown frozen at –18°C. After thawing, consume within 24 hours and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Stuffed jalapeno pepper is a spicy pepper filled with cheese, meat or vegetables, often baked or fried. Originating from Mexico, jalapenos have a bright, slightly fruity flavor and moderate heat that is softened by the stuffing.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The jalapeno gets its name from the Mexican city of Xalapa, where it was first cultivated.
Capsaicin levels in jalapenos typically range from 2,000 to 8,000 Scoville Heat Units, making them moderately hot compared with other varieties.
Stuffed jalapenos are commonly served as “jalapeno poppers,” a popular bar snack in the United States.
There are many stuffing options: cream cheese, cheddar, ham, seafood, as well as vegetarian blends of beans and quinoa.
Jalapenos are rich in vitamin C and carotenoids, which give them their vivid green color.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains capsaicin
items.content: Capsaicin may boost metabolism and has mild analgesic properties.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: One stuffed pepper provides about 50‑70 kcal, making it a good option for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Carotenoids and vitamin E protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Spiciness
items.content: Very hot fillings can irritate the stomach of sensitive individuals.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: If the stuffing contains cheese, people with lactose intolerance or dairy protein allergies may react.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared stuffed peppers are often salted; those with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Skin irritation
items.content: Capsaicin can cause skin irritation on contact; wearing gloves while preparing is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stuffed jalapenos can be served hot or cold. They are often baked until the cheese melts and paired with sour cream or guacamole. Ideal as a bar appetizer, they can also be added to salads, sandwiches, or used as a pizza topping.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared stuffed peppers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in freezer‑safe bags for up to 2 months. Reheat in the oven or microwave before serving.

yogurt-ns-as-to-type-of-milk-fruit.title: Yogurt, NS as type of milk, fruit

content.title: About
content.content: Yogurt is a fermented dairy product made by culturing milk with specific bacterial strains. The NS (lactose‑free) version is suitable for people with lactose intolerance. Fruit additions provide natural sweetness and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Yogurt has been known since ancient Mesopotamia more than 5,000 years ago.
Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus work together to create yogurt’s characteristic taste and texture.
Fruit‑flavored yogurts often contain a small amount of natural sugars, making them popular with children.
Lactose‑free (NS) yogurt is produced by adding lactase, which breaks lactose down into glucose and galactose.
Regular consumption can support gut health thanks to probiotic bacteria.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: Live bacterial cultures help maintain a balanced gut microbiome and support the immune system.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Yogurt provides a substantial amount of calcium essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Protein contributes to muscle repair and promotes satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yogurt supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low‑fat option (NS version)
items.content: Lactose‑free yogurt often has reduced fat content, making it suitable for diet‑focused eating.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to casein or whey proteins.

items.title: Added sugar in fruit flavors
items.content: Fruit‑flavored yogurts can contain added sugars; people monitoring glucose should check labels.

items.title: Probiotic sensitivity
items.content: Those with compromised immune systems may experience discomfort from live cultures; consult a healthcare professional.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Yogurt can be enjoyed on its own, blended into smoothies, used as a base for sauces, dressings, or desserts. Fruit pieces add extra flavor and nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store yogurt in the refrigerator at 2–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
